title: The Conservative Advantage
coreMove: Separate breadth of moral vocabulary from virtue, truth, or policy quality.
sourcePressure: The chapter argues for a politically sensitive conservative advantage in moral-register breadth, not blanket moral superiority.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer turns the conservative advantage into a team scoreboard.

sourceAnchors.name: the conservative advantage
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar defines the claim as broader moral-register reach, not simple moral superiority.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The advantage is a bigger moral keyboard in certain public arguments, not a certificate of virtue.

sourceAnchors.name: moral foundations framework
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says the chapter builds on the political application of multiple moral foundations.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Once more foundations are on the board, the winning message may be the one that plays more than two notes.

hook: Do not open ch08 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: progressive housing campaign broadening its message
exampleSpecs.audience: organizers whose case speaks mostly harm and fairness
exampleSpecs.stakes: James adds neighborhood loyalty and order without abandoning tenant protection.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: James rewrites one mailer to protect renters and long-time neighbors in the same paragraph.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Rain has softened the stack of door hangers on the campaign office sill.

exampleSpecs.domain: conservative criminal justice reform group speaking to skeptics
exampleSpecs.stakes: Chiara keeps authority and loyalty in the reform argument instead of copying liberal language.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Chiara asks the sheriff which sentence lets him support reform without betraying order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Do not make him choose between mercy and order," Chiara says.

exampleSpecs.domain: public health team improving vaccine outreach in mixed counties
exampleSpecs.stakes: Akira adds duty, protection, and local loyalty to a safety message.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Akira removes a scolding headline and replaces it with a county duty frame.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: County maps and clinic schedules cover the breakroom table.

exampleSpecs.domain: labor party candidate trying to reach veterans
exampleSpecs.stakes: Lukas sees why fairness-only language misses service, loyalty, and authority.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Lukas compares two stump speeches and marks the foundations the losing one never touched.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Lukas one veterans' breakfast to hear the missing notes in the speech.

exampleSpecs.domain: corporate ethics rollout after a supplier scandal
exampleSpecs.audience: executives needing a message beyond compliance
exampleSpecs.stakes: Camille builds a message that speaks purity, loyalty, and fairness without moral grandstanding.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Camille turn a legal memo into a pledge employees can recognize across foundations.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You notice the supplier memo folded beside a box of recalled parts.

exampleSpecs.domain: school funding coalition combining tax and tradition appeals
exampleSpecs.audience: coalition writers in a politically mixed town
exampleSpecs.stakes: Andrew tests whether the message plays only fairness or also stewardship and local pride.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Which version would Andrew's mixed-town audience repeat at a diner table?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Which sentence can travel from the PTA meeting to the hardware store?

skillTargets: separate moral-register breadth from moral goodness
evaluate a message by how many foundations it can speak to
avoid caricaturing liberals or conservatives while explaining asymmetry

tryThisNowSpec: Take a message you support and add one moral register it currently ignores, without changing the policy claim.
